Nvidia: Jensen Huang resigns with immediate effect after 33 years at the helm of the chip giant; the stock drops more than 13% at the open

Nvidia's board announced on Thursday, November 12, the immediate resignation of its CEO, Jensen Huang, brought down by a scandal over affairs, one of them with a woman suspected of spying for China. CFO Colette Kress is taking over on an interim basis. The stock lost as much as 14.4% on Wall Street [1][3][4].

On Thursday, November 12, Nvidia's board announced that Jensen Huang was stepping down as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately; Reuters was the first agency to break the news [1][2].

Colette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer, becomes interim CEO while keeping her finance role, until the board picks a permanent successor [1]. She has run the group's finances since 2013 [3].
The board also appointed Harvey C. Jones as its chair, a first in the company's history [1]. The official statement gives no reason for the departure [1].

According to the New York Times, as cited by the San Francisco Chronicle, the departure follows the revelation of a second affair, with a Nvidia executive [6]. Jensen Huang had already admitted to a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese national whom US intelligence suspects of spying for Beijing [3][7].
On the stock market, the share fell to $148.80 shortly after the open, down 14.4% from Wednesday's close, before paring its losses during the morning [4][5].
Research firm Bernstein halved its price target, from $400 to $200 [5]. According to Quartz, the stock has lost nearly $750 billion in value since the scandal began [8].

Harvey Jones says he has "full confidence" in Colette Kress and that operations and product plans will continue [1]. The board repeats that it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, and its inquiry goes on [7]. Colette Kress pledges to "build on the foundation" Jensen Huang laid over 33 years [7].

Key point: the boss most closely associated with the rise of artificial intelligence is leaving, overnight, the company that makes most of the chips behind AI, five days before its quarterly results [1][3].

The affair unfolded within days: on November 8, the board opened an independent inquiry after Jensen Huang admitted to an affair, and three Republican House committee chairs asked him for a closed-door briefing on November 18 on Nvidia's safeguards against adversary powers [9]. The revelation of a second relationship precipitated his exit [6].

The shock goes beyond Nvidia: its stock carries heavy weight in major US indices and in AI-focused funds, and the loss of nearly $750 billion in value in a few days, according to Quartz, affects millions of savers [8]. The Chinese side of the affair is part of the rivalry between Washington and Beijing over chips [3][9].
What comes next hinges on two milestones: the November 17 results, the first without Jensen Huang, and the choice of a successor, internal or external [3][1].

If you hold a US or global index fund (an S&P 500, Nasdaq or "World" ETF), Nvidia is one of its biggest holdings: its fall weighs on your savings even if you don't own the stock. It's also a reminder that a company closely tied to one person can lose a lot over a governance scandal, not just over its sales. This is information, never advice to buy or sell.

How it works: why a CEO's exit sinks the stock

A share price reflects what investors expect from future profits. When a company is closely associated with its leader, they wonder whether strategy, relationships with major customers and the ability to innovate will hold up without them: this is "key-person risk". An abrupt departure, with no successor groomed, raises uncertainty; analysts then revise their price targets, as Bernstein did by halving its own [5]. The board tries to reassure by quickly naming an interim chief the markets know, here the CFO, and by stating that projects will continue [1].
Precedents: executives who left over a relationship that broke the rules
June 2018
Brian Krzanich steps down as head of Intel after the revelation of a past consensual relationship with an employee, in breach of the group's internal policy [10].
Breaking an internal rule can be enough to force out a CEO, even without financial misconduct [10].
September 1, 2025
Nestlé fires its chief executive, Laurent Freixe, after an inquiry into an undisclosed romantic relationship with a direct subordinate; Philipp Navratil replaces him [11].
The board investigated and then acted fast, naming a successor right away to reassure [11].
